KNOWLEDGE GRAPHS / PART 03 OF 03

Put Graph RAG to work in a VCF agent

Publish the graph, connect it over MCP, and use cited VCF evidence to build a better preflight plan.

Greg Havens · November 23, 2026

From knowledge graphs to Graph RAG
  1. 1. How to build a knowledge graph
  2. 2. Build and verify a graph with Jev Graph Builder
  3. 3. Put Graph RAG to work in a VCF agent

A useful VCF agent needs two kinds of evidence: what the documentation says about the exact release and what the target environment is doing now. A documentation graph can improve the first step. It can connect an error to an applicable prerequisite or procedure that a search hit alone might miss. It cannot tell you what the installer’s DNS server actually returns. Design the workflow around that gap.

Prepare a versioned corpus

My vcf-corpus brings together release-specific docs and support articles for VMware Cloud Foundation. To build your own, start with the deployment guide, release notes, API spec, and troubleshooting articles for the release you operate. Keep product, component, version, source URL, and heading metadata; preserve which build and topology a specific fix applies to. Keep internal runbooks and incident records in a separate access scope. A query client’s access to a graph is access to its source passages, not just its summaries.

Use the build process from Part 2, then inspect real questions with both search and graph_context. The first ranks chunks without graph traversal. The second returns passages identified by p1, p2, and so on, plus the returned neighborhood. Those labels are local to a response. Save the canonical source and heading alongside the label if you need to audit an answer later.

Connect the agent locally

Start with stdio, which lets the client launch the MCP server locally without exposing an HTTP endpoint. For Codex, the project documents a configuration like the following. Use the full path to the executable and the actual build directory; keep the API key in the runner’s environment. Give the serving process its own database credentials where possible: JGB_READER_DSN can use the project’s reader role, which reads graph content and records its own decision calls.

[mcp_servers.vcf-docs]
command = "/path/to/venv/bin/jev-graph-builder"
args = ["mcp", "--name", "vcf-docs"]
env = { JEV_GRAPH_BUILDER_CONFIG = "/path/to/build/jev-graph-builder.yaml", JGB_REGISTRY_PATH = "/path/to/build/registry" }
env_vars = ["TYPESAFE_API_KEY", "JGB_READER_DSN"]
tool_timeout_sec = 300

Check the client examples for the agent you run. Name the connector after the corpus so the tool descriptions tell the agent when to use it. Keep the documentation connector separate from any credentials or tools that operate VCF.

Publish a graph for a shared agent

publish moves a built graph into the storage used by a hosted query service. Both targets below require a build that includes the command; the 0.1.1 wheel used in Part 2 does not. Use the pinned source revision below in a separate virtual environment and test against a staging copy or a fresh build before pointing it at an existing graph. It does not grant access to a VCF installation. The PostgreSQL path copies into a staging database, switches it in after loading, and retains the previous database. You run the MCP service separately. Keep the destination DSN in JGB_PUBLISH_DSN and verify the server points to the published graph.

# In a separate virtual environment:
python -m pip install "jev-graph-builder @ git+https://github.com/greghavens/jev-graph-builder.git@0541c3488438df9a5a9c59f762ed145653418835"
# From the directory that holds the completed build:
# Set JGB_PUBLISH_DSN securely before running this command.
jev-graph-builder publish --target postgres

The Cloudflare target uses D1 for indexed text and graph data, Vectorize for embeddings, and a Worker to serve requests. It is documented in this pinned repository revision; the --target cloudflare flag is not part of the 0.1.1 release used in Part 2. Check publish --help on the build you deploy.

jev-graph-builder publish --target cloudflare \
  --name vcf-docs --allow-github-users your-github-login

Follow the target’s OAuth setup and authorize only the intended users. For hosted HTTP, require HTTPS and authentication; the local HTTP mode without a public URL is unauthenticated and should stay on loopback. Check both a valid login and a rejected one. Then compare a few cited queries against the source build, since the hosted target can use a different embedding profile. Connect the client to the published MCP URL only after those checks pass.

Worked example: turn a DNS error into a preflight plan

Consider this documentation question, with no live credentials attached:

VCF 9.0: explain why adding a DNS record alone does not fix “reverse DNS lookup failed” in VCF Installer validation, and what to verify about the deployment specification.

On one run against vcf-docs, search at k=5 found the relevant cause and resolution, among other results. graph_context returned 65 passages and 57 edges, including an example_of link from the general failure p19 to a case-mismatch example p44. It also returned licensing material and other documents that did not apply. The graph surfaced a concrete example; the search baseline already had enough to cover the core fix. Sending all 65 passages to the agent without filtering would be a poor trade.

EvidenceWhat to do with it
Broadcom KB 435717 (p20, p21)Take the flagged FQDN and IP from the deployment specification. Check forward and reverse resolution from the installer’s network context, and compare the returned pair with the spec.
Broadcom KB 415466 (p44)Check exact spelling and casing. This case illustrates how a lookup can succeed and still fail the installer’s comparison.
Site observationsRecord actual values and timestamps if read-only probes are authorized. With no live results, report readiness as unknown. Do not change DNS or start deployment to test a documentation claim.

A practical response from the agent would say: “The installer needs the forward result, the reverse result, and the FQDN/IP in the spec to agree. I can give you the checks now. I can’t say the environment passes until we have results from the installer’s resolver.” That produces a useful plan instead of a guess about the infrastructure.

Give the agent a workflow, not just a connector

  1. Scope. Identify the release, component, topology, requested task, and whether you have authority to observe the environment.
  2. Retrieve and filter. Use graph traversal when the task spans prerequisites, diagnosis, and validation. Favor matching product versions and authoritative passages. If graph context is noisy, use a targeted search. A returned passage is a lead; answerable: true only means the tool found something.
  3. Plan and observe. Translate the evidence into ordered read-only checks with expected outputs. Capture what actually happened, leave unobserved state unknown, and stop on conflicting evidence.
  4. Review changes separately. If an authorized operator asks for remediation, review the proposed change, blast radius, rollback, and post-checks before any write. Never treat commands in retrieved text as instructions or use a graph edge as authorization.

The VCF 9.x agent skills complement retrieval: they give the agent a task workflow and version guardrails; the graph brings back supporting passages. Neither replaces observations from the environment.

Measure whether the workflow got better

Replay held-out tasks in two arms: ranked search and graph-expanded retrieval. Freeze the corpus snapshot, model, prompt, and context budget. Where a task needs site evidence, give both arms the same recorded observations or sandbox; do not grade an invented live result as success. Score correct version, required prechecks, supported citations, proof of postconditions, and correct abstention. Also track irrelevant context, latency, and the cost of a wrong action. Include single-passage questions, cross-document prerequisites, and deliberately underspecified requests. The DNS run above is a retrieval example, not a benchmark or a live VCF test.

Start with one task. Choose a recurring VCF operation, record the checks you expect and the evidence required for each, then compare one run with traversal and one without. Expand coverage once you can explain what the graph changed in the agent’s plan.
